docs.title: Home
docs.text:
trappyframe is a low-cost and open-source microscopy system that is highly customisable. It is an inverted low-magnification system (1-2X) that is built on a 3D printed opto-mechanical cage system, simple optics, and the Raspberry Pi Hardware ecosystem. This system was build for parallelisation. Multiple units can be assembled, mounted, and operated in parallel. The microscope can be printed and assembled in any laboratory/school/home with a few simple tools.

The microscope is primarily designed to track motile algae. However, it can be used as it is or customised for any general microscopy requiremnt.

Instructions on parallelisation, including the assmmbly of a Raspberry Pi cluster/bramble can be found in the parallel project Trappy-Scopes/raspberry_shrub. The control layer software can be found in the parallel project Trappy-Scopes/trappyscopes and instructions to configure it for trappyframe can be found in the here.

docs.title: Assembly instructions
docs.text: ---  How to assemble the trappy-scopes microscopes in easy to follow 100 steps:  1. Take a **baseplate** and mount the Rasperry Pi HQ Camera on the pegs using M2-10mm screws (X4). Remove the tripod mount from the camera as it is not required. We recommend long CSI cables (24" from Adafruit 1731). Pass the CSI cable from the slits to the camera connector. Prefer using a side which is adjacent to the **flexures**. Connect the cable (it should pass under the Baseplate and to the camera. Do not twist the cable and handle it gently.) The connectors (shiny-side) should face up towards you when you connect them to the camera.  2. Take four 6mm diameter 50cm Stainless steel rods. You can get your own cheaper ones or buy from ThorLabs. Mount them to the baseplate and tighten the flexures using M4-10mm screws. Make sure that there is no imbalance and the rods are evently inserted. You should consider additional steps to improve rod adhesion to the baseplate:     1. Use a bit of stanard electrical tape at the end of the rods to improve fitting.     2. Additional headless-screws that can be mounted (holes already inbuilt.) TODO-add screw specifications     3. Use a strong glue at the baseplate to bond the rods to the plate.  3. Mount the baseplate on an **M6 breadboard** temporrily to aid assembly. We recommend a smaller breadboard for the assemby.  Subsequently the unit should be transported to its final place after certain assembly steps. M6-10mm screws are recommended for this.  4. Add the **Lower-Tube lens mount** (has a smaller central hole compared to the Upper-Tube mount) to the frame from the top (The flexure side should align with the flexure side of the baseplate).  5. Add the **zoomlens** to the mount without taking of its covers.  6. Add the **Upper-zoom lens mount**. The zoomlens should snuggly align with mounts. We will connect it to the camera and align it later.  7. Add the **midplate** to the frame and place it approximately near the knulred ring of the zoomlens.  8. Assemble the **sample stage**:     1. The magentic mount sample stage needs to be assembled beforehand. It used four 1.9mm high 6.2mm diameter magnets in a cylinder form-factor. The magnets should directly fit in their respective holes. But since 3D printing is not an exact science, we can use the help of some glue. Use only sufficiently enough glue and fit the magents in place. Decide which pole should stay up and stick with it! Do not randomly place the magents.      2. If you used glue, let it dry for a sufficent time. Clean the stage of any access glue beforehand.     3. If you plan to use any additional peripherals that mount from below, you should also install the magents under the stage in the same prescribed way.     4. Add the sample mount to the assembly (align the flexures!). Z-position is irrelvant. Place it above the tubelens ofcourse.  9. Add the **asphere/condensor mount** to the assembly (align the flexures!). Check this part specifically for imperfections on the inside. Clean it, if required.  10. Add the **ED/illumination mount** to the assembly sans the LED clip. Pick a conventional side for the slit and stick with it (extra careful in aligning the flexures! Todo-explain more.  11. Assemble the **top plate**:     1. Add two magnets (the centre should be sufficient). Follow the same rules as the **sample stage**.     2. Add it to the saaembly.  12. Attaching the camera to the tubelens: it helps a lot to be clean. Clean the dust. Wash your hands and wear gloves if you can!     1. Lift the componets gently until there is some space bwtween the camer and the tubelens.     2. Remove the caps first from the tubelens and then the camera. Bring the two componets close and they should perfectly align! If they don't then you made a mistake somewhere. Cover the camera immediately and start again. Remember to choose the apropriate adapter (the HQ camera comes with both C and CS mounts.)     3. Rotate the tubelens very slowly as access speed causes friction and that chips off small pieces of metal that contaminate the camera surface.     4. Turn until you can't and ensure that the tube lens is firmly mounted on the camera.     5. Move the upper and lower zoomlens mount plate to fix the tubelens properly.     6. Use eight M4-10mm screws to fix both the plates in position.     7. Sometime, the alignment mark on the tubelens gets shaded by the box, so better add a haptic cue, like a piece of coarse tape that you can feel. 13. Assmble the **trappybox side sections** (the long ones) (M3-5mm screws):     1. Take the back-side and mount it on the topplate (central and a side screw).     2. Now add the central screw on the baseplate. Screwing is difficult but not immpossible. If its too difficult for you, then leave it for the end!     3. Now try and align the midplate with its respective screw holes (first the center and then a side one).     4. Repeat these steps for the front side  (long one)!     5. Add extra screws to improve the stability, these many should work fine.      6. With the last steps, we have also properly aligned the midplate and the topplate, so fix them with M4-5mm screws.     7. Unscrew the scope assembly from the breadboard (all four screws). But keep the screws there. Release the screws that connect the box to the baseplate to release some tension. Now attach the small flaps with one M3-5mm screw each on the baseplate. Do not tighten it, keep them such that they are like a flap. You can skip this step if you have no space constrains!     8. No put the scope on its designated position and tighten the M6 screws again! Tighten them well! It's permanent. You should be able to access the screws through the flaps.     9. Pass the CSI cable to the SoC (RPi 4B or smth) and tug the extra cable between the tubelens and the box. Now tighten the small portions of the box and fix them. If you have many CSI cables that are overlapping, insulate them further with Aluminium foil or something, or there will be a lot of interferance.     10. Add the pico board that connects to LEDs and the temperature sensor on top of the topplate. There is a breadboard and standard M2.6 screws should work well.     11. Now add an appropriate temperature and humidity sensor (swinging near the sample stage and run the wires through the top plate flexure on your left side).     12. On the right side. Add a closed Rod support clamp and use two M3-20mm screws and M3 nuts to secure them.     13. Assembling the LED climp complex:        1. TODO     14. Connect the sensors and LEDs to the RPi Pico based controller. Make sure to connect to the right pins and keep the connections tight.  # Models

docs.title: Disassembly Instructions
docs.text: Whether you want to replace the unit, change a part, or reconfigure the scope structure, disassembly is required.

docs.title: Disassembling everything
docs.text: This is easy. Remove all the components one by one. It helps to have the scope mounted on a breadboard.

docs.title: To unmount the whole scope without complete disassembly
docs.text:
1. Remove both the left–right bottom box panels.
  2. Loosen the bottom M3 screws on the front and back panels so that the acrylic can bend slightly, allowing easier access to the M6 screws holding the scope. Small M3 Allen keys are useful, as the working space is limited.
  3. Disconnect the camera cables using a small screwdriver to reach the clamps on both sides.
  4. Gently pull the acrylic panels so they do not block the heads of the M6 screws, then loosen the M6 screws completely. Move diagonally to prevent stress accumulation on one side: bottom-left → top-right → bottom-right → top-left.

docs.title: Change configuration without unmounting
docs.text:
1. Remove the rod clamps.
  2. Remove all the M3 screws that connect the box panels to the Top Plate.
  3. Disconnecting the electronics is not strictly necessary, as the Top Plate can be removed while still connected to the LED and the temperature and humidity sensor.
  4. Move the parts slowly without applying shear force. Use lubricant if necessary.

docs.title: Electronics & Optics
docs.text:
Optics and electronics can be customised to the specific needs. This note in particular covers the use of a commercial Tube-Lens as a low-magnification objective. The Tube Lens is coupled to a Raspberry Pi HQ Camera, which connects to a Raspberry Pi SoC. For electronics, we describe a universal controller framework based on the Raspberry Pi pico microcontroller that can be used to control illumination, and temperature senosors.

The microcontroller plateform allows for arbitrary customisation. This topic is developed separately in the Trappy-Scopes/electronics which contains instructions on how to assemble very simple eletronic circuits. Most of the magic happens in code and the micropython firmware for the microcontroller platform can be found in the Trappy-Scopes/pico_firmware.

We use Raspberry Pi 4B, however Raspberry Pi 5 and to some extent lower models are also fine. We recommend using a high RAM version — 8GB. This needs to be coupled with a microSD card, we reommmend a decent 128GB card. Higher memory can be unstable, but upto 128GB works well and has been extensively tested. We will also need connector cables, which are listed in the Bill of Materials page.

docs.title: Calibrations
docs.text: Calibration is central to the correct operation of scientific instruments. Without calibrations, measurements from sensors are meaningless numbers. Here we present a suite of calibrations to characterize each microscope, which uses a general structure followed across all Trappy-Scopes instruments. The role of the calibrations is to characterize each instrument correctly and to also summarize how identical instruments diverge from one another.

docs.title: How a calibration works
docs.text:
Every calibration has two halves: acquisition on the scope, then gathering and analysis on a computer.

flowchart LR
    A[Acquisition script on each scope] --> E[Experiment folders]
    A -. some scripts .-> L[Calibration stored on the scope]
    L --> X[Later experiments]
    E --> N[Notebook: gather and analyse]
    N --> R[Results in the notebook]
  • Acquisition runs on the scope. The scripts live in trappyscopes under scripts/. Each run produces an experiment folder.
  • Gather and analyse is a Jupyter notebook in the calibrations/ folder of this repository, one notebook per calibration. It gathers the experiment folders with trappy-explorer and contains all of its own maths, so it reads top to bottom.
  • Results are computed in the notebook. Some scripts also store the calibration locally on the scope, for regular use by later experiments.

docs.title: What each calibration page contains
docs.text: Section What it says Purpose The question the calibration answers Protocol The acquisition script, the setup, and how long it runs Data The files and columns a run produces Gather and analyse The notebook Results One row per scope Acceptance The values a scope should meet Persistent records How many records the calibration writes onto the scope

docs.title: Running a notebook
docs.text:
Every notebook page has two buttons: Download notebook and Open in Colab.

  • In Colab, the first code cell installs what Colab lacks and asks for a .zip of your experiment folders. For large data, mount Google Drive instead and set DATA to the folder.
  • On your own computer:
cd calibrations
pip install -r requirements.txt
jupyter lab

Set DATA at the top of the notebook to your own experiment folder. Each page cites the runs it was made from by experiment ID. That data is not published, so use your own.

docs.title: Persistent records
docs.text: Some calibrations store their result on the scope itself, in the device's shelve (~/<device name>, written through hive/physical.py), so later experiments can use it. Each page states how many records it writes.

  • kernel.log, and in raw/ the stress-ng log and YAML, every sysbench output and the scope's config.txt.

def flags(t):
    """Throttle flags raised during the run: 'now' bits, and 'since boot' bits not set at the start."""
    v = t.throttled.dropna().astype(int).to_numpy()
    if not len(v):
        return "unknown"
    seen = np.bitwise_or.reduce(v)
    during = (seen & 0xF) | ((seen >> 16) & 0xF & ~(v[0] >> 16 & 0xF))
    return ", ".join(n for i, n in enumerate(NAMES) if during >> i & 1) or "none"

docs.title: CPU and RAM health¶
docs.text:
Does a scope's board compute correctly, keep its full speed and stay cool under a sustained full load? This notebook reads one standard one-hour run per scope, gives each board a verdict, and compares processor and memory speed across the fleet.

Analysis written by Claude (Anthropic); conceptualised and verified by Yatharth Bhasin.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text:
Acquisition: scripts/debug/cpu_ram_health.py, protocol cpu_ram_health/2. install_requirements() once per scope (stress-ng, sysbench and smartmontools, with apt), then create_exp() and start(). No acquisition may run at the same time. About 2 h 8 min per scope:

  1. Settle, 60 s idle. Refused if anything else uses more than 10% of the CPU.
  2. Speed, sysbench, 3 × 20 s each: CPU on 1 and on 4 threads; RAM write and read on 4 threads with 16 MiB blocks, larger than the 1 MiB L2 cache, so the RAM is measured and not the cache.
  3. Stress, stress-ng, 120 min: 4 CPU workers cycling through every CPU method, plus 1 memory worker cycling through every memory pattern on a fixed 5 GiB. Every result is checked against the known answer (--verify).
  4. Cooldown, 2 min idle.

Clock, throttle flags, SoC temperature, fan, memory and swap are logged once a second throughout, the SSD's own temperature sensor once a minute (the test puts no load on the SSD, so any rise is heat from the board), and the kernel log is kept. The parameters are fixed in the script; a run with any of them changed is marked non-standard. Protocol /1 had a 60 min stress phase and no SSD temperature; both versions can be read here.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: Runs are read with trappy-explorer's legacy reader, explorer.legacy.ExpExplorer. Only folders with KIND in their name are used, so DATA may hold other runs too. One row per run. The speed stream has one row per sysbench repeat (test, unit, repeat, value).

docs.title: Boards¶
docs.text: What each board is and how it is set up. Identical boards should show the same kernel, firmware and bootloader. A scope that differs here is the first place to look when its numbers differ below.

docs.title: Speed¶
docs.text: Each test's result as a percentage of the fleet median (the median over scopes of each scope's median), one point per repeat. Identical boards sit within a few percent of zero. A scope below zero in every repeat is slower; repeats far apart from each other point to something else running during the test. The table gives each scope's median in the test's own unit (events/s for CPU, MiB/s for RAM).

docs.title: Temperature through the run¶
docs.text: SoC temperature (30 s mean) against time since the start of each run: the speed tests in the first minutes, the hour of stress, then the cooldown. The curve should rise, settle to a plateau and fall back at the end. The Pi 4 starts slowing itself down at 80 °C. A plateau that keeps climbing, or one far above the other scopes' at the same room temperature, points to the cooling: fan, heatsink or airflow.

docs.title: Cooling¶
docs.text: Left: the plateau, the mean SoC temperature over the last 10 min of stress, above the room temperature read by the scope's T&H sensor at the start and end, so that scopes in warmer or cooler spots compare. Right: how fast the board cools once the load stops: the time constant τ of an exponential fitted to the cooldown, decaying towards the board's idle temperature before the run. τ is the time it takes to lose 63% of the excess heat; a smaller τ is better cooling.

docs.title: Clock under load¶
docs.text: Every clock reading during the stress phase. A healthy board holds its configured clock (arm_freq) the whole time. Readings below it mean the firmware capped or throttled the clock, for heat or for a low supply voltage; the throttle flags in the results say which.

docs.title: Memory¶
docs.text: Available memory and swap in use through the run. The memory worker holds a fixed 5 GiB during the stress phase, so available memory drops by about that much and comes back at the end. Some swap while plenty of memory is still available is normal Linux behaviour under this load. Swap that keeps growing, or available memory near zero, means something else holds memory.

docs.title: SSD temperature¶
docs.text: The SSD's own temperature sensor, read once a minute, against time since the start of each run. The test puts no load on the drive, so a rise is heat from the board next to it. Some drives report a fixed value instead of a live reading; a flat line that never moves, at the same value on every drive of that model, is one of those. Runs recorded before protocol /2 have no SSD temperature.

docs.title: Results¶
docs.text: One row per run, also written next to each run's data (analysis/cpu_ram_health.yaml) and exported to results/. wrong_results: stress-ng log lines reporting a wrong result. kernel_faults: kernel errors during the run (oops, segfault, lockup, RCU stall, SError); blank if the kernel log was not captured. throttle_during: throttle flags raised during the run, or none. ssd_*: the SSD temperature summary from above. clock_held_pct: share of stress-phase clock readings at arm_freq. *_pct: speed against the fleet median. verdict follows the acceptance table below; script_verdict is what the script recorded on the scope.

docs.title: Acceptance¶
docs.text:
Per board:

Criterion Level stress-ng reports a wrong result (exit 2, or a fail: line in its log) FAIL A kernel error during the run FAIL The run stopped early, stress-ng exited with another error, memory ran out, or a speed test gave no result INCOMPLETE Under-voltage during the run WARN: check the power supply and cable before the board Clock capped or throttled, or below arm_freq in more than 1% of the stress-phase readings WARN SoC at 80 °C or more WARN Kernel log not captured WARN

FAIL means a board fault: replace the board, or rerun to confirm. INCOMPLETE means rerun. Speed is not judged; it is compared across the fleet. Swap is reported but not judged: holding 5 GiB makes the kernel swap briefly on healthy boards too. The script counted swap as a WARN in protocol /1, so for those runs script_verdict can say WARN where verdict says PASS. SSD temperature is reported, not judged.

docs.text: This calibration writes 0 records to the scope. Its set-up step, install_requirements(), installs stress-ng and sysbench with apt; nothing else on the scope changes.

docs.title: Fleet clock synchronization¶
docs.text:
How far apart are the scopes' clocks? A disturbance recorded on several scopes can only be lined up in time if their clocks agree. This notebook puts a bound on the clock difference between any two scopes, from repeated runs. The clocks are not made perfect; their error is measured.

Analysis written by Claude (Anthropic); conceptualised and verified by Yatharth Bhasin.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text:
Acquisition: scripts/debug/fleet_clock_synchronization.py. One NTP server gives time to every scope over the wired network. Each scope runs chrony with that server as its only time source; install_requirements() sets this up once per scope. Each run then logs what chrony measures for 2 h, and the runs on all scopes overlap. The whole run is repeated at least three times (N ≥ 3). As in Lab Streaming Layer, clock offsets are measured and stored next to the data, and the error is worked out afterwards.

Recommended: make sure the NTP server is itself well synchronized before the run.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: The run is repeated: each repeat is one folder holding one run per scope. SETS lists the folders, oldest first; below they are R1, R2, ... Runs are read with trappy-explorer's legacy reader, explorer.legacy.ExpExplorer, in legacy mode: the script writes plain numbers only, so nothing is dropped. Each run has four streams in experiment.yaml: setup (what the clock follows, at the start and the end), ntp (one row per clock update from the NTP server), pico (the Pico's clock, once a minute) and tandh.

docs.title: Maximum error¶
docs.text:
chrony bounds how far the scope's clock can be from true time (UTC):

max error = |offset| + root dispersion + root delay / 2

Most of it is the NTP server's own distance from UTC, which is the same for every scope and cancels between two scopes. The server's own root delay (server_root_delay_s) is removed. Its root dispersion is kept: chrony reports the root dispersion of the sample it trusts most, often an older one, while the server's dispersion grows between its own updates, so the latest server_root_dispersion_s is too large to subtract (in tests 1 and 2 that gave a negative error 41-75% of the time). The error against the NTP server is then an upper bound, high by the server's root dispersion (0.3-2.2 ms in tests 1 and 2):

error to server = |offset| + root dispersion + (root delay - server root delay) / 2

docs.title: Scope to scope¶
docs.text:
At every 10 s tick, two scopes' clocks differ by at most the sum of their errors against the NTP server. Over the time all runs of a repeat overlap, each map shows the value this bound stays below 99% of the time, one map per repeat. This holds when every server address belongs to the same NTP server, as here; otherwise compare against UTC instead.

The colour scale runs from 0 to the acceptance limit (ACCEPT_MS). The differences between pairs are not a property of the scopes: they do not repeat from one repeat to the next. What holds for the fleet is the fleet bound, in the table below the maps: at each tick, any two scopes differ by at most the sum of the two largest errors at that tick; the fleet bound is its 99th percentile over the repeat.

docs.title: Each NTP exchange¶
docs.text: Every clock update: the offset measured to the NTP server, and the round-trip network delay to it, per scope and coloured by repeat (each scope's server address is in the runs table). The delay shows the quality of each scope's network path; large offsets come from slow exchanges.

docs.title: The Pico's clock¶
docs.text:
Each scope's Pico keeps its own clock, and nothing synchronizes it. The run reads it once a minute over the serial link: as found for the first 5 min, then sets it once to the scope's time (UTC) and follows it. Each reading is a request and reply timed to the moment the Pico's seconds tick over, with an error of a few ms (error_s). This is for information and is not part of the acceptance. A Pico keeps its clock until it loses power, so it is found either as set by an earlier run, or restarted at 2021-01-01 (about -1.85e8 s).

As found: the board, whether its clock counts fractions of a second, and how far its clock was off at the start of each repeat (found_s, + = ahead).

docs.title: Results¶
docs.text: Per run: one row per repeat and scope, also written next to each run's data (analysis/fleet_clock_synchronization.yaml). err_*_ms is the error against the NTP server (the upper bound above); utc_p99_ms is chrony's own bound against UTC; longest_gap_s is the longest time between two clock updates; accepted: the scope's own error stays below ACCEPT_MS / 2 for 99% of the run. pico_*: how far off the Pico's clock was as found (s, + = ahead), its offset right after it was set (ms), its drift (ppm) and how far it moved after the set (ms). fleet_bound_ms is the repeat's fleet bound.

docs.title: Acceptance¶
docs.text: The fleet passes when the fleet bound, how far apart any two scopes' clocks can be for 99% of a repeat, stays below ACCEPT_MS = 4 ms in every repeat. 4 ms is a tenth of one frame at 25 fps, so a disturbance seen on two scopes falls in the same frame. Each scope's own share is ACCEPT_MS / 2: the dashed line in the first figure, and accepted in the results.

docs.title: Persistent records¶
docs.text: This calibration writes 0 records to the scope. Its set-up step, install_requirements(), does change the scope's time service: chrony replaces systemd-timesyncd, with the NTP server as its only source. The run also sets each Pico's clock to UTC once; the Pico loses that setting when it loses power.

Allan deviation. Average the signal over windows of length τ and ask how much one window's average differs from the next. Where noise is random, longer windows average it away and the curve falls; where slow drift takes over, longer windows see more of it and the curve rises. The minimum is the best stability the scope reaches, and the averaging time that gives it. Read the plot from left to right: the falling part is noise, the rising part is drift. Pure white noise falls as 1/√τ.

def disturbances(s, k=8):
    x = S[s].set_index("wall")

docs.title: LED + camera intensity fluctuations¶
docs.text:
How steady is the illumination, as each scope's camera sees it? This notebook measures the noise, drift, fluctuation timescales and disturbances of the per-frame mean intensity over a 16 h run, on every scope.

Analysis written by Claude (Anthropic); conceptualised and verified by Yatharth Bhasin.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text: Acquisition: scripts/longterm/intensity_continuous.py. The red LED is held at a fixed control voltage and the camera records continuously at 25 fps. Frames are encoded and discarded; only the mean of each colour channel is kept, per frame. The LED driver is PWM at 3 MHz, so the PWM itself averages out within each 18 ms exposure. The trap should be empty.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: Runs are read with trappy-explorer's legacy reader, explorer.legacy.ExpExplorer. Extended parsing keeps tuple attributes such as the LED voltages. M1–M4 saved no run attributes.

docs.title: Correction for runs recorded before 16 Nov 2026¶
docs.text:
Until trappyscopes 29bca5b, intensity_continuous wrote the last ~30 s of each run to intensities.csv twice. For runs started before that fix, the second copy is dropped here. This applies to those runs only: in a later run, repeated timestamps stop the notebook instead.

Separately, for every run, T&H rows reading exactly 0 are dropped: older scripts wrote 0 for a failed reading, and a real reading is never 0.

docs.title: Overview¶
docs.text: Each panel is one scope's red intensity, averaged over 1 min and shown as % from its own median. The bottom panels show the temperature at the scopes in each column (M1–M4 left, M5–M8 right), so drift can be compared with temperature by eye. In this run M1 and M7 ran under different conditions from the rest; M1 had cells loaded in its trap and sits at a different focal position.

docs.title: Noise¶
docs.text: floor_pct is the frame-to-frame noise, std(Δr)/√2, which drift does not affect. g_dark and b_dark are the green and blue channels under red light: crosstalk and dark level. From here on, the first 30 min of each run are left out.

docs.title: Drift¶
docs.text: tempco_pct_per_C is the change in red intensity per °C of temperature at the scope, from 5 min means. Over one night both fall or rise slowly, so a high correlation is expected whatever the cause; a deliberate temperature step would test it.

docs.title: Temperature removed¶
docs.text: Red intensity is fitted against the temperature at the scope (5 min means) and the fitted part is subtracted. If the drift is mostly temperature, the corrected curve (colour) is flat compared with the measured one (grey). Over one night anything else that changes steadily is removed with it. Runs from 2026-11-13 on also record the camera-sensor and CPU temperatures (cam_temp_c, temp_c in the telemetry), which can be used the same way.

docs.title: Timescales¶
docs.text: Power spectrum. How the fluctuation power is spread over frequency. Each spectrum is fitted with A·f^(−α) + B: a 1/f-type part (α ≈ 1 is flicker noise) and a white floor B. The corner frequency is where the two are equal. Sharp lines above the fitted curve are periodic disturbances.

docs.title: Disturbances¶
docs.text: Three kinds: spikes (a frame far from its 1 s running median; bursts within 1 s count once), steps (the median of the next minute differs from the previous minute's), and gaps (more than 100 ms between frames).

docs.title: Acceptance¶
docs.text: None. This calibration characterises each scope and writes nothing to it, so there is no pass or fail.

docs.title: Persistent records¶
docs.text: This calibration writes 0 records to the scope.

def fit(g):
    (m, c), cov = np.polyfit(g.V_pwm, g.pfd, 1, cov=True)
    res = g.pfd - (m * g.V_pwm + c)
    ss_res, top = (res ** 2).sum(), m * g.V_pwm.max() + c
    ss_pe = g.groupby("level").pfd.apply(lambda y: ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()).sum()
    L, N = g.level.nunique(), len(g)
    F = ((ss_res - ss_pe) / (L - 2)) / (ss_pe / (N - L))

                      "readings_per_level": N / L, "lof_p": stats.f.sf(F, L - 2, N - L)})

docs.title: LED control voltage vs sample intensity¶
docs.text:
How much light reaches the sample for a given LED control voltage, on each scope and for each LED colour? A light meter at the sample plane reads the light while the control voltage is stepped. A straight line per LED then converts control voltage into photon flux density (PFD, µmol/m²/s). The acquisition script stores that line on the scope, for later experiments.

Analysis written by Claude (Anthropic); conceptualised and verified by Yatharth Bhasin.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text:
Acquisition: single_channel_calibration() in scripts/calibration/control_volt_vs_sample_intensity.py.

  • Light meter: lux1, a TSL2561 on a Seeed Grove Digital Light Sensor, read by its own Pico at 16× gain and 101 ms. It sits on a 4.5 mm centring plate in the sample holder, about 5 mm above the sample-holder plane, and is moved from scope to scope.
  • Sweep: one LED colour at a time, from 0 to 2.9 V in 0.1 V steps, first with the beacon off and then on. Each point waits 0.2 s, then takes one reading.
  • Repeats: since trappyscopes 21b83ff each sweep runs four times (up, down, up, down), about 16 min per scope. Earlier runs swept up once per beacon state.
  • PWM: the LED driver is PWM at 3 MHz, which gives 42 duty levels, so the light changes in steps of 3.3/42 V whatever voltage is asked for.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: Runs are read with trappy-explorer's legacy reader, explorer.legacy.ExpExplorer. Each run has one stream per LED colour (red, green, blue), one row per reading. Each run also records what the light meter reported about itself (devices/lightmeter/config), and the fit the script stored on the scope (devices/<colour>/params).

docs.title: Sweep labels for runs recorded before 17 Nov 2026¶
docs.text: Until trappyscopes 3252c69, the script swept each colour once with the beacon off and once with it on, both upwards, and recorded no sweep or direction. For those runs the two sweeps are numbered here in the order they were taken. In a later run, missing labels stop the notebook instead.

docs.title: The light meter¶
docs.text:
The conversion constants hold only for the chip, gain and integration time they were measured for. They come from the TAOS TSL2560/TSL2561 datasheet (TAOS059N, March 2009), TSL2561T/FN/CL column:

  • Re_640nm: ch0 counts per µW/cm² at 640 nm, 16× gain, 101 ms (typical). The same table allows 750–1250 counts for a nominal 1000, so the absolute scale is good to ±25% between chips. Scope-to-scope comparisons do not depend on it, because one sensor measures every scope.
  • colour_factors: ch0 responsivity at each LED's peak wavelength relative to 640 nm, read off Figure 4.

Each run's sensor report must match.

docs.title: Which LED each channel lights¶
docs.text: The sensor's second photodiode (ch1) sees mostly near-infrared, so the ratio ch1/ch0 depends on the wavelength: highest for red, low for green, lowest for blue. Each point is one channel on one scope, at 1 V and above. A channel whose ratio sits with another colour lights that colour's LED. From here on each channel is analysed as the colour it actually lights; the table lists any that differ from their name.

docs.title: PWM levels¶
docs.text: The control voltage sets a PWM duty cycle. At 3 MHz on the Pico's 125 MHz clock there are 42 levels, and MicroPython 1.25 rounds each requested duty to the nearest one. The plot shows the voltage asked for against the voltage the PWM actually produces: equal steps would lie on a straight staircase; uneven steps are where two 0.1 V requests land one level apart or two. The fits below use the produced voltage.

docs.title: Raw readings¶
docs.text: Sensor counts (ch0) against the control voltage, every reading, one panel per scope, coloured by the LED each channel actually lights. Readings that sit on top of each other were repeatable. The flat start is the LED below its threshold; the small steps along each line are the PWM levels.

docs.title: Photon flux density¶
docs.text: ch0 counts give the irradiance at the sensor, E = counts / (Re_640nm × colour factor) µW/cm². For a narrow-band LED the photon flux density is PFD = E[W/m²] × λ[nm] / 119.6 µmol/m²/s, with λ each scope's own lambda_nm for that colour. Readings at the sensor's full-scale count are the ceiling, not the light, and are left out of the fits; the table counts them.

docs.title: Fit¶
docs.text: One straight line per scope and colour, PFD = slope × V + intercept, against the produced voltage, over all readings from level 3 (about 0.2 V) up; below that the LED gives no light. resid_sd_pct is the scatter about the line as % of the PFD at full scale. The lack-of-fit test compares how far the readings at each level sit from the line with how far they sit from each other: lof_p below 0.05 means the line misses by more than the readings scatter, i.e. the response is not quite straight.

docs.title: Hysteresis¶
docs.text: At each level, the mean of the readings taken on the way up minus those taken on the way down, as % of the PFD at full scale. Zero means the light does not depend on the direction of approach. A consistent sign means the LED (or the light meter) lags: on the way up readings come out low if the light has not settled, on the way down high. Runs without a downward sweep cannot show this.

docs.title: Repeatability and the beacon¶
docs.text:
repeat_pct: the spread of all readings at the same level (std / mean), median over levels from 1 V up, where one count is below 0.1% of the reading.

beacon_pct: how much higher readings are with the beacon on than off, median over the same levels. The beacon-on sweeps always come after the beacon-off sweeps, so this also contains any drift between them. beacon_dark_counts separates the two: it is the beacon's own light, read with the LED off (levels 0 and 1), beacon on minus off. Near zero means the beacon adds no light at the sample, and any beacon_pct is drift.

docs.title: Fleet¶
docs.text: Each scope's slope (PFD per volt) for each colour. Scopes on a horizontal line deliver the same light for the same control voltage; distance from the others is how much a scope needs its own calibration.

docs.title: What the script stored on the scope¶
docs.text:
The script fits its own line when the run ends and stores it on the scope, one per channel. It fits against the voltage asked for, over every reading including the dead zone. This table compares the stored line's prediction with this notebook's fit at 1 V and 2 V asked for. The light at a requested voltage is that of the PWM level it lands on, so a line fitted against the requested voltage is off by up to half a step there.

Green and blue convert to PFD almost identically with this sensor (λ divided by the colour factor is about 577 for both). So a channel that lights the other of those two colours still stores a line that is right for the light it delivers; only its colour is wrong.

docs.title: Acceptance¶
docs.text: This calibration writes to the scope, so it needs limits. The checks are: the light meter matches the constants (checked above), no saturated readings, each channel lights the colour it is named after, and the hysteresis, repeatability and fit residual stay within limits. The limits are not set yet; the values are in the results table.

docs.title: Persistent records¶
docs.text: This calibration writes 3 records to each scope: the shelves of its red, green and blue channels (~/red, ~/green, ~/blue). Each holds the fitted line (calib_slope, calib_intercept, calib_cov_matrix), the readings it was fitted on (calib_volts, calib_counts, calib_pfd), calib_dt, calib_sensor_gain, the light meter's report (calib_sensor), the constants used (calib_constants), and the run that produced it (calib_eid, calib_exp_dir).

The two streams hold one row per Pico (picos) and one row per Pico per step (steps). Each run folder also holds the files the analysis uses:

  • calls.csv: every call, with step, requested rate_hz, device, latency_ms, outcome (ok, timeout, error, wrong) and, from script 7e26f77 on, the board's uptime pico_ms.
  • events.csv: recoveries, drills and injected faults, one row each.
  • system.csv: once a second, the Pi's throttled flags and whether the scheduler thread is alive.
  • pico_stress.json: the run's summary, including drill times and the scheduler results.
  • kernel.log: kernel messages. It starts with the kernel's buffer, so it reaches back before the run.

docs.title: Pico link stress¶
docs.text:
How reliably does a scope talk to its Picos, and how many Picos can one machine drive? This notebook measures the round trip of a call to every Pico on a scope as the call rate rises, the most the link does flat out, how fast a lost link comes back, and what a hung call or a broken job does to the scheduler that every recording uses.

Analysis written by Claude (Anthropic); conceptualised and verified by Yatharth Bhasin.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text:
Acquisition: scripts/debug/pico_link_stress.py, create_exp() then start_acq_blocking(). No acquisition may run at the same time. The short run takes about 4 minutes with one Pico.

Every Pico plugged into the scope is tested at once: the ones the scope mounted at start-up as they are, any other one connected directly by its port. Nothing else needs to be wired to them. Each call is one round trip through the production path (SerialMPDevice → raw REPL), sent from exp.schedule: it toggles the onboard LED, adds two random numbers and returns the sum with the board's uptime. The sum is checked.

The steps, in order: a ramp of requested rates per Pico (1–50 calls/s); a burst of back-to-back calls; two drills per Pico (close and reconnect the port, then machine.reset() and wait for the board to come back); a job that raises inside exp.schedule; a job that blocks it for 10 s; and a call that never returns, which the recovery ladder has to clear (wait, Ctrl-C, soft reset, reconnect, hard reset). To map how the link scales, run it with one Pico plugged in, then another one alone, then both together.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: Runs are read with trappy-explorer's legacy reader, explorer.legacy.ExpExplorer. One row per run; n_picos is how many Picos the run tested.

docs.title: Response time as the call rate rises¶
docs.text: Each line is one Pico in one run, through the ramp steps. Left: the 99th percentile of the round trip at each requested rate; a line that bends upward marks the rate at which calls start to queue. Right: the rate the calls actually ran at. exp.schedule checks for due jobs every 10 ms, so the achieved rate falls below the requested one as it nears 50 calls/s even on a healthy link. A step at a low rate has few calls, so its p99 is close to its single slowest call.

docs.title: Round-trip times¶
docs.text: The distribution of the round trip of every good call in the ramp and the burst, on a log axis. A curve that rises steeply in one place means a steady link. A tail stretching to the right is calls that waited: for the USB bus, for the Pico, or for the scheduler.

docs.title: How many Picos can one machine drive?¶
docs.text: The phase space: rows are the number of Picos a run tested, columns the requested rate per Pico, pooled over every scope and run. Left: the 99th percentile round trip. Right: the fraction of calls that failed. A row needs runs with that many Picos plugged in; the cells where the colour changes are the limits of one machine. Below: the most calls per second the machine got through flat out (the burst), summed over its Picos, one point per run.

docs.title: Recovery¶
docs.text: How long each way back took, one point per Pico per run: closing and reconnecting the port, a machine.reset() until the board answers again, and a call that never returns until the ladder has the board answering again (the first step waits late_reply_s for a late reply before it acts). The table gives the same times and the ladder step that cleared each hung call.

docs.title: The scheduler¶
docs.text: Every recording runs its periodic jobs on exp.schedule, one thread. The run injects a job that raises and a job that sleeps for schedule_hang_s. The table shows, per run, whether the raise killed the thread, how many Pico calls ran after it, whether the boards still answered a direct call, how many calls ran once the thread was restarted, and the longest any Pico waited while the scheduler slept.

docs.title: USB and power¶
docs.text: The kernel log is searched for every USB port a Pico has used. pico_usb_drops_in_run counts the disconnects on those ports during the run; each machine.reset() drill causes exactly one, so any more is a Pico that dropped off the bus on its own. pico_usb_drops_in_log counts them over the whole log, which reaches back before the run. throttled lists every value of the Pi's throttled flags seen during the run; 0x0 means no under-voltage and no thermal throttling.

docs.title: Acceptance¶
docs.text:
Per Pico, per run:

Criterion Level Any call timed out, errored or came back wrong, apart from the one injected hang FAIL The board could not be recovered (fatal) FAIL A reconnect or machine.reset() drill did not bring the board back FAIL The recovery ladder did not clear the injected hang FAIL A Pico dropped off USB other than in the reset drill FAIL The Pi reported under-voltage or throttling (throttled flags other than 0x0) FAIL A ramp step was not clean: p99 above p99_limit_ms, or a failure or recovery in it WARN

The scheduler results are reported but not judged: they describe exp.schedule, which is the same code on every scope.

def cache(w, drop=0.5, win=32):
    """GB written before the 32-chunk speed first falls below half the opening speed, and the speed after it."""
    s, gb = w.write_s.to_numpy(), w.cum_gb.to_numpy()
    roll = win * CHUNK_MB / pd.Series(s).rolling(win).sum().to_numpy()

        return np.nan, len(s) * CHUNK_MB / s.sum()
    cut = below[0] - win // 2
    return gb[cut], (len(s) - cut) * CHUNK_MB / s[cut:].sum()

docs.title: Storage health¶
docs.text:
Can each scope's drives hold a continuous recording, and are they healthy? This notebook measures the sustained write speed of the experiment SSD and the OS SD card, how long single writes take, whether a 15.7 MB/s recording would keep up, and whether everything written reads back intact.

Analysis written by Claude (Anthropic); conceptualised and verified by Yatharth Bhasin.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text:
Acquisition: scripts/debug/storage_health_statistics.py, create_exp() then start_acq_blocking(). No acquisition may run at the same time. About 60–70 min per scope.

The SSD gets up to 20 files of 9.45 GB (one real 10-minute split each), written in 64 MiB chunks with an fdatasync after every chunk, so each timing is the drive's and not the page cache's. Writing stops before the drive is 85% full. Every chunk is then read back and checked against its CRC. The SD card gets one 1 GB file. SMART is read before and after, with the drive idle; fstrim runs at the end; all test files are deleted.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: Runs are read with trappy-explorer's legacy reader, explorer.legacy.ExpExplorer. One row per run.

docs.title: Write speed as the drive fills¶
docs.text: Most SSDs first write into a fast cache (flash used one bit per cell), then slow down once it is full. A flat line at the start that drops to a lower one shows where the cache ran out, and the lower line is the speed a long recording actually gets. Repeated swings between high and very low speed mean the drive pauses to empty its cache while still writing. A scope with no run in DATA gets an empty panel. A drive that starts slow has no cache to run out of, and its cache size is left blank.

docs.title: How long single writes take¶
docs.text: The distribution of the time each 64 MiB chunk took to reach the drive, on a log axis. A curve that rises steeply in one place means a steady drive. A long tail to the right is stalls. One chunk holds about 4.3 s of video at 15.7 MB/s, so chunks slower than that are moments the drive fell behind real time.

docs.title: Would a recording keep up?¶
docs.text: A recording produces 15.7 MB every second. While one chunk takes t seconds to write, the recording adds 15.7 × t MB and the drive takes one chunk away. Count how much would be left waiting. Zero means the drive kept up. Tall or long peaks are data a recording would have to hold in memory until the drive caught up.

docs.title: Read-back¶
docs.text: Every chunk is read back from the drive, not from memory, and checked against its CRC. One point per file; the box shows the median and interquartile range for each scope. The USB bridge, not the flash, usually sets the ceiling here, so drives behind the same bridge should line up.

docs.title: Acceptance¶
docs.text:
Per scope, for the experiment SSD:

Criterion Level Any chunk reads back wrong (CRC) FAIL SMART not PASSED, or reallocated, pending, media or link-CRC errors rose during the run FAIL A kernel storage error or reset on the drive during the run FAIL Speed after the cache runs out below 3 × 15.7 = 47 MB/s FAIL A 15.7 MB/s recording would have more waiting than the page cache holds before Linux throttles writers FAIL A 15.7 MB/s recording would have more than 2 s of video (31 MB) waiting WARN

WARN is informational: this test bypasses the page cache, but a real recording writes through it, so anything below the page-cache room (page_cache_room_mb, read from the scope's vm.dirty_* settings) is absorbed without the recording ever waiting. TRIM and the SD card figures are reported but not judged: most USB bridges do not pass TRIM, and the SD card holds the OS, not recordings.
